result:
The proposed answer 1/3 is wrong. The construction it relies on only gives an upper bound of 1/3, and a better construction gives an upper bound of 1/5.

**Counterexample construction.** Let H be any plane triangulation on s vertices. It has 2s−4 faces. Inside each face abc, add two vertices x and y: join x to a, b, c, and join y to x, a, b. This keeps the graph a triangulation (each face adds 2 vertices, so 2 interior vertices per face contribute 4 new faces, with all faces triangles). The resulting graph G has

n = s + 2(2s−4) = 5s − 8

vertices.

**Upper bound on λ.** Let S be the original s vertices. Each pair {x, y} is a connected component of G−S with exactly 2 vertices, since its only outside neighbours are a, b, c in S. A P₃ cannot lie inside a 2-vertex component, so every P₃ contains a vertex of S. Hence λ ≤ s.

Therefore λ/n ≤ s/(5s−8) → 1/5 as s → ∞, so c ≤ 1/5 < 1/3.

**Why the proposed reasoning missed this.** The argument used only isolated vertices of G−S. That gives λ ≤ n − α, and with α ≈ 2n/3 this yields about n/3. It ignored components of size 2, which are cheaper for the adversary to build: each one attaches to three S-vertices, and planarity allows about 2s components, so one can have n ≈ 5s rather than n ≈ 3s.

The optimal value may be below 1/5 with more elaborate constructions, so I have not determined c exactly. But 1/3 is not it.

VERDICT: REJECT

CONFIDENCE: 4
